report:
## Correction: The evidence does not support "yes"

Based on the strongest available evidence, **arthroscopy (arthroscopic surgery) does not meaningfully help knee osteoarthritis**—the answer to this question is actually **no**, not yes.

**Key evidence:**

1. **Landmark placebo-controlled RCT (Moseley et al., NEJM 2002):** In this trial, patients with knee OA were randomized to arthroscopic debridement, arthroscopic lavage, or sham surgery. Outcomes for pain and function were no better after actual arthroscopy than after placebo surgery at any point up to two years (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259).

2. **Follow-up RCT (Kirkley et al., NEJM 2008):** In patients with moderate-to-severe knee OA, arthroscopic surgery plus optimized physical/medical therapy provided no additional benefit over optimized physical/medical therapy alone (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333).

3. **Cochrane systematic reviews:** Both the original review of arthroscopic debridement and the updated 2022 review of arthroscopic surgery for degenerative knee disease concluded that arthroscopy probably does not improve pain or function compared to placebo or non-surgical care (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD005118_arthroscopic-debridement-osteoarthritis-knee; https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease).

4. **International clinical guideline (BMJ, 2017):** An international expert panel, based on a systematic review of 13 trials (~1,700 patients), issued a **strong recommendation against** arthroscopic surgery for degenerative knee disease, citing lack of lasting benefit and potential harms (https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982/).

**Conclusion:** High-quality, sham-controlled trials and systematic reviews consistently show arthroscopy does not provide meaningful benefit for knee osteoarthritis beyond placebo or conservative therapy; major guidelines now recommend against it.
